initial.title: Recovering from partial automation means one workflow, not the whole business
initial.body:
If you are recovering from partial automation, do not start by asking, “What AI can we add back?” Start by naming one workflow that was partly automated, then stalled, broke, or was abandoned. Invoice data entry, lead follow-up, and customer FAQ replies are all different problems; mixing them together is how small automations turn into little maintenance hobbies.

The bounded decision is simple: only keep investing if the workflow is still repeatable, measurable, and frequent enough to justify the setup work. That 8–10 hours-a-week pain point you may recognise is only a persona example, not a promise or a benchmark. If the underlying process has changed, a broken automation may just need to stay broken.

One practical diagnostic question is: who approves the output? If the answer is always “me” or “a person”, AI-assisted automation may fit. If the answer is “nobody checks it”, or the system would run without review, you need explicit controls before you trust it. Human approval stays mandatory for money movement and other high-risk decisions.

The next step is manual and boring on purpose: pick one half-broken workflow, write down in two sentences what still happens by hand and where the automation failed, then mark whether the output needs human approval. If you cannot answer that cleanly, the problem is scope, not software. We build inside the owner’s own tools and accounts, so the finished system stays with you; that is policy, not magic.

selected_lessons.application: The task explicitly prohibits a CTA ('CTA rule: None'). L01 requires treating diagnostic invitations as CTAs unless authorised. Since no CTA is authorised, the post must end with a neutral practical observation or actionable next-step note—not a booking prompt—and avoid any implicit invitation to contact Bareni.

steps.instruction: Define 'recovering from partial automation' as a single, repeatable workflow where automation exists but is incomplete, stalled, or broken. Ask the owner to name one specific task (e.g. invoice data entry, lead follow-up, customer FAQ response) that is partially automated or abandoned. Frame this as the diagnostic question that precedes any decision.

Explain the boundary condition honestly: automation is worth investing in only if the workflow is repeatable, measurable, and occurs frequently enough to justify setup time. Use the persona scenario (8–10 hours per week of repeated work) as a reference point, not a guarantee. State that some broken automations should stay broken if the underlying workflow has changed.

Describe one practical diagnostic: ask 'Who approves the output?' If the answer is always 'me' or 'a person', the workflow fits AI-assisted automation. If it is 'nobody checks it' or 'it runs without human review', the workflow is higher-risk and requires explicit controls. Link this to the evidence boundary: human approval is mandatory for money movement and other high-risk decisions.

Explain the no-lock-in positioning without legal warranty language: if the owner decides to proceed, Bareni builds the system inside their own tools and accounts (SaaS, automation platforms, databases in the owner's name from the start), so the owner is never trapped and can hand off or retake control. Relate this to the Bareni delivery model and scope.

State the next step concretely: identify one half-broken or abandoned workflow, write down (in two sentences) what currently happens manually and where the automation failed, and assess whether the output needs human approval. Do not invite a call or diagnostic booking; frame this as a standalone thinking exercise the owner can do now.

Close with a neutral technical observation—e.g., 'Most small-business automation failures happen because the original scope was too loose or the approval rule was never defined, not because the technology broke'—that positions future action as optional but informed. Avoid scarcity language, pressure, or any CTA.

constraints_to_preserve.handling: Do not name, attribute results to, or invent any customer, team member, deployed project, financial outcome, or savings figure. Use only Bareni's self-built demos and stated service model as examples.
Do not recommend unsupervised automation for money movement or high-risk decisions. Emphasise human approval requirement in the diagnostic step.

Preserve the frozen persona (plain-speaking technical expert, founder-to-founder), the approved evidence boundaries (no invented capabilities beyond C01–C05), and the human-approval mandate. Do not soften scope discipline or invent future roadmaps.
Use plain, direct English. Keep examples (the persona scenario, the synthetic demos) clearly distinct from observed results. Do not make unsupported claims about productivity, cost, or outcomes.

evidence.quote: The diagnostic identifies the one recurring workflow, says honestly whether AI fits

Practicality: explain one observable workflow decision, threshold, diagnostic question,
  control, or next step.

ledger.rationale: This is a writing instruction proposing a definition and a diagnostic question for the reader, not an assertion of current implementation or observed use. It fits the approved diagnostic framing of identifying one recurring workflow.
ledger.use_guidance: Keep as a proposed framing and diagnostic question addressed to the reader. Use generic task examples (invoice data entry, lead follow-up, FAQ response) without implying any customer, deployment or observed case.

evidence.quote:
The representative pains are 8–10 hours a week of repeated customer questions, neglected sales leads,
  and manual invoice/data work. The 8–10 hours is a persona scenario, not a market
  statistic or observed customer result.

have a frequent, repeatable workflow with a
  measurable outcome

ledger.rationale: The core (repeatable, measurable, frequent workflows are the fit criterion; 8–10 hours is a reference point) matches approved evidence, but the claim says only "not a guarantee" and does not state that the 8–10 hours is a persona scenario rather than a market statistic or observed result.
ledger.use_guidance: Add the qualification that 8–10 hours per week is an illustrative persona scenario, not a market statistic, measurement, or observed customer result. Also present the fit criteria as Bareni's current scope discipline, not a universal rule.

evidence.quote: Human approval is mandatory for money movement and other high-risk decisions.

amount-based human-only approval,
  refusal of agent approval/payment attempts

ledger.rationale: The 'Who approves the output?' test is a proposed diagnostic question for the reader rather than a report of an existing feature or observed use; it aligns with the approved human-approval boundary.
ledger.use_guidance: Keep as a proposed diagnostic question. State the human-approval rule for money movement and high-risk decisions as current policy; do not imply the approval test is an automated product feature or has been applied with customers.

evidence.quote:
Finished code is handed to the customer. Database, automation-tool, and API
  accounts are in the customer's name from the start. Retainer support is optional.
  Describe this as policy and no-lock-in positioning, not an absolute legal warranty.

Bareni works
  inside the customer's environment and delivers a working system.

ledger.rationale: The core account-ownership and no-lock-in positioning is supported, but the wording "never trapped" states an absolute outcome that the evidence explicitly restricts to policy rather than an absolute warranty.
ledger.use_guidance: Add the qualification that this is Bareni's working policy and no-lock-in positioning, not an absolute or legal guarantee; replace "never trapped" with a measured statement that accounts and finished code stay with the owner. Do not imply an existing customer relationship.

evidence.quote: Task:** Turn the abstract topic into a bounded Bareni workflow decision. Explain one practical next step.

ledger.rationale: This is a permissible instruction proposing a manual, self-directed next step for the reader, and it respects the no-CTA rule by excluding any invitation to book a call.
ledger.use_guidance: Keep as a proposed manual exercise the reader performs themselves. Do not add any booking invitation, diagnostic offer, or conversation prompt; keep it distinct from any Bareni-run service.

evidence.quote:
Numbers require a source and status. Keep observed results, estimates, targets,
  synthetic data, and examples distinct. Never invent a benchmark, guarantee, ROI,
  saving, revenue lift, productivity result, or thesis-validated capability.

never imply customers, deployments, outcomes, savings, revenue lift,
  production readiness, or capabilities beyond the supplied evidence

ledger.rationale: The proposed closing sentence asserts a current general fact about why most small-business automation failures happen. No approved source supports any observation of failure causes or their frequency; Bareni has no customer or field data, so the statement would be an invented empirical generalisation.
ledger.use_guidance: Exclude the 'most failures happen because...' assertion. A separately supported neutral close is available: state as Bareni's own scope discipline that a pilot needs a defined scope, fixed price, measures, and a named approval rule, framed as how Bareni bounds work rather than as an observed failure pattern. Keep the no-CTA and no-scarcity requirements.

selected_lessons.text: For informational marketing content, treat any invitation to book a diagnostic, discuss the situation, or continue the conversation as a CTA unless the task explicitly authorises one. End with a neutral practical observation or next-step note instead of a meeting prompt.
